elements.element: No minimum purchase/volume commitment imposed on Customer
elements.evidence: "Customer has no minimum purchase or take-or-pay commitment."

elements.element: Fees payable only for usage or ordered Services
elements.evidence: "Customer pays only for Services it actually orders or uses under an Order Form."

elements.element: Any commitment limited to the current 12-month term
elements.evidence: "may not exceed the then-current twelve-month term"

elements.element: Commitment reducible by Customer on 30 days' notice
elements.evidence: "may be reduced by Customer on thirty days' written notice"

elements.element: Shortfall settled by true-up rather than penalty
elements.evidence: "any shortfall is settled by a true-up of the unpurchased amount rather than a penalty"

offending_extra_words: Any volume commitment must be set out in an Order Form, may not exceed the then-current twelve-month term, may be reduced by Customer on thirty days' written notice, and any shortfall is settled by a true-up of the unpurchased amount rather than a penalty.
reasons: The locked target is preferred, and the first two sentences alone fully achieve it: no minimum/take-or-pay commitment and payment only for Services ordered or used.

The third sentence imports the entire fallback bargain (12-month cap, 30-day reduction right, true-up) into a preferred-level cure, mixing the two levels and adding roughly 40 unnecessary words; the fallback belongs in the margin comment (where it is already offered), not the operative text.
Official minimality gates fail: word expansion ratio 2.48 (>1.50) and changed-character ratio 0.880 (>0.600) — the edit is a whole-clause rewrite where a tighter replacement would suffice.

Intent is preserved: no undefined terms are introduced (Order Form and Services are defined), no free-standing reduction or termination rights are created, and the mild tension between "no minimum ... commitment" and "Any volume commitment must be set out in an Order Form" is not an operative contradiction.
